skill.name: Repetition that holds a text together
skill.why: Repeated key words link sentences, so readers know they're still on the same thing.
skill.how: Spot the word that keeps coming back, plus other words for the same thing.

beats.say: Writers repeat key words on purpose.
beats.show: The **ladder** was old. Nobody trusted the **ladder**.

beats.say: The repeat tells you it's still the same thing.
Writers also use other words for that same thing.
beats.show: The **storm** hit at noon. The **blizzard** raged all night.

beats.say: Together they make a chain. It holds the text together.
Follow the chain, and you'll know what the text is about.

encounters.frame: The Chorrawong found this article in the school newsletter. It hummed along.
encounters.text:
THE ORCHESTRA ON THE MOUNTAIN

The orchestra from Scaffold Peaks Primary has just finished its first ever tour. Its thirty players visited three schools in three days, carrying their instruments up and down more than two hundred ladders. Every player had to pack a beanie, two pairs of gloves and a very good attitude.

The orchestra's first stop was Pine Gully, where the hall was so cold that the trumpets froze to the players' lips. Nobody was hurt, but the first song was mostly squeaks. The trumpet players spent the rest of the day drinking warm water through straws.

The orchestra's second stop went much better. The players warmed their instruments by the fire before they started, and the audience asked for three encores. One parent said it was the best concert she had heard in years.

The orchestra finished the tour at home, playing to a packed hall. The principal cried. The caretaker danced. The conductor says that next year they will tour by helicopter.

encounters.frame: Indi wrote this report for the Scaffold Peaks Gazette. The Chorrawong has a suspicion about the thief.
encounters.text:
THE CASE OF THE VANISHING SUNFLOWERS

Last Thursday, the Ridge Gallery reported that its most valuable painting, a bright yellow canvas of sunflowers, had disappeared overnight. The small stone building sits on a ledge halfway up Crag Tower, and its only door had been locked from the inside. By morning, the masterpiece was gone, and the security guard was baffled. He said he had checked every room at midnight, and nothing had been out of place. Police searched every corner of the gallery. They found no footprints, no broken windows and no sign of a ladder. The only clue was a single yellow feather on the floor beneath the empty frame. It was Wren who solved the mystery. She noticed that the feather belonged to a young sulphur-crested cockatoo, and that a small window near the ceiling had been left open for fresh air. The next day she climbed the cliff above the building and found a nest. There, woven neatly into the twigs, was the missing artwork, torn into strips and arranged in a perfect yellow circle. The feathered burglar, it seems, simply liked the colour. The gallery has decided not to press charges. The cockatoo has declined to comment. Indi has offered to paint a replacement, in a slightly less tempting shade of blue.

encounters.frame: Tully gave this speech to the Snowcats the night before the grand final. The Chorrawong was in the front row.
encounters.text:
Twelve months ago, we finished last. We lost every game but one, and that one was a draw against a team with eleven players. People laughed at us. Some of you nearly quit. I nearly quit. But Coach Ana told us something I have never forgotten. She said that climbing these peaks isn't about the whole ladder. It's about the next rung. One more rung.

So we trained in the snow. We ran the towers before breakfast, and we ran them again after school. We did push-ups in the hut while Mo cooked dinner, which, if you've tasted his cooking, was the easy part. When our legs were screaming, we said it to each other: one more rung.

In round nine, we were down by thirty points at half-time. Nobody gave up. We clawed back one goal at a time, and we won by a single point. One more rung.

Tomorrow we play the Rams, who haven't lost all year. They're bigger. They're faster. They've won three flags in a row. I'm not going to stand here and promise you we'll win. I'm going to tell you what we'll do. When it hurts, when we're behind, when the crowd goes quiet, we'll take one more rung. And then another.
